figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Why a Euclidean KD-tree mis-prunes on non-Euclidean spaces. (a) On $SO(2)$ the query and its true nearest neighbor lie a short geodesic arc apart across the $\pm\pi$ seam but at opposite ends of the split coordinate, so the Euclidean point-to-cut bound prunes the far child, whereas the wrap-aware bound (2) measures the wrapped distance and explores it. (b) A quaternion block, on a cross-section of $S^{3}$: the node box $R_{B}$ covers the arc its subtree occupies and is far from $v$ but close to the antipode $-v$, the same rotation, so pruning on $d(v,R_{B})$ alone would discard it. The bound is the smaller of the two ambient point-to-box distances, $G_{B}=\min(d^{2}(v,R_{B}),d^{2}(-v,R_{B}))$, reflecting the query, never the box; it is admissible because every $p\in R_{B}$ has $d^{2}(v,p)\geq d^{2}(v,R_{B})$ and $d^{2}(-v,p)\geq d^{2}(-v,R_{B})$. Products follow blockwise, and for $S^{n}$ ($n\geq 2$), its chordal metric is the ambient one.
figures.headline: A Euclidean bound prunes the true neighbor across the wrap seam or quaternion antipode, while the proposed bounds keep it.
citing_sentences: 1(b)), matching MPNN’s per-node block bound while storing no per-node box (it is reconstructed, not stored) and leaving the Euclidean update and node layout unchanged.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Head-to-head vs. prior exact-manifold NN libraries (single thread, $k=1$). All methods are exact for their own metric. On pure $SO(3)$, where all three share one ground truth, nigh’s intrinsic bound is fastest, but the proposed block-level bound now beats MPNN and stays within a small factor of nigh. The $SE(3)$ panel compares two exact solvers of different product metrics (see Table III) on the same workload, so it reports cost, not ranking quality.
figures.headline: On SO(3), the proposed tree queries in 15 µs versus 45 µs for MPNN, trailing nigh's fastest intrinsic partition.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Loop-closure retrieval, KITTI 00 top-down: markers are keyframes whose candidate set from the naive (sign-continuous) tree is wrong ($w_{R}{=}15$). The failures concentrate on the revisited streets, i.e. exactly where loop closures are found. Only the proposed index is exact, at every $w_{R}$ (Table IV).
figures.headline: Loop-closure candidates from the naive sign-continuous tree are wrong at revisited streets, while the proposed index is exact at every weight.
citing_sentences: The naive tree falls to $0.44$ (sign-continuous) and $0.92$–$0.99$ (canonicalized; canonicalization merely moves the seam), with errors concentrated on revisited streets ($25\%$ of KITTI 00 and $65\%$ of DCC01 queries get a wrong candidate set, Fig. 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Incremental index vs. alternatives on the sliding-window KITTI workload ($4.8$ M-point map, $k{=}5$; single thread except the async variant’s background rebuild and ikd-Tree’s, which is always on). Top: CDF of per-frame update latency (steady state). Bottom: physically stored points; the synchronous tree stays within $1.3\times$ the live set, while the Bentley–Saxe forest never reclaims trimmed points.

abstract: Nearest-neighbor (NN) search underlies countless robotics algorithms, but many state spaces are not Euclidean: orientations live on $SO(2)$ or $SO(3)$ and poses on $SE(2)$ or $SE(3)$, and a Euclidean KD-tree on their raw coordinates returns wrong neighbors. We present a header-only, dependency-free C++ KD-tree library for exact NN search on user-defined product manifolds declared at compile time: the space is composed from base manifolds ($\mathbb{R}^{n}$, $SO(2)$, $SO(3)$, $S^{n}$; products $SE(2)$, $SE(3)$, tori) with a single type alias, and the library synthesizes a metric whose pruning is provably admissible, wrap-aware for circular coordinates and double-cover-aware for unit quaternions. Experiments confirm exactness (recall $1.0$ vs an exhaustive scan under the same product metric), where the Euclidean-on-raw shortcut collapses to recall $\approx 0.5^{m}$ for $m$ rotation blocks, with up to three orders of magnitude speedup over brute force. We further contribute an incremental, self-balancing single-tree index for points under heavy churn (e.g. sliding-window LiDAR maps) or $SE(3)$ trajectories: bounded memory and faster updates than prior work, with an optional asynchronous tail-latency-bounding mode. The implementation is open source: https://github.com/jlblancoc/nanoflann.

sections.body: The paper presents a header-only, dependency-free C++ KD-tree for exact nearest-neighbor search on product manifolds such as SO(2), SO(3), SE(3) and tori. The user declares the space at compile time with a single type alias. A Euclidean KD-tree on raw coordinates returns wrong neighbors, and its pruning silently discards true neighbors across wrap-around seams. Prior exact manifold trees, MPNN and nigh, hard-code a fixed set of spaces and store topological state per node. This work instead synthesizes a pruning bound that is admissible for each coordinate's topology, with the proof given as Lemma 1.
sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.headline: Exact nearest-neighbor search on non-Euclidean robotics spaces needs a general, dependency-free KD-tree rather than planning-specific libraries.

sections.body: Related work covers Euclidean KD-tree libraries such as FLANN, ANN, libnabo and PCL, all of which operate on Euclidean coordinates. General-metric structures such as VP-trees and cover trees treat the metric as a black box, so every pruning test needs a full metric evaluation. The closest prior work is exact manifold KD-trees. MPNN applies a topology-aware bound on products of R, S^1 and RP^3. Ichnowski and Alterovitz give an intrinsic SO(3) scheme, extended in nigh. The section states three differences: the quaternion bound needs no per-node storage, the factor set is open at compile time, and the code ships in a general-purpose library.
sections.heading: RELATED WORK
sections.headline: Prior exact manifold KD-trees hard-code their space sets and store per-node topological state, which this work avoids.

sections.body: This section recaps the Euclidean KD-tree the library builds on. Points are indexed by a permutation array and split along the dimension of largest spread. Each interior node stores only the split dimension and two scalars, divLow and divHigh, with no per-node bounding box. Search is branch-and-bound. A running lower bound B on the squared distance to the far child is updated in O(1) when the search enters that child. In Euclidean space the per-dimension term is the squared gap to the split value. Generalizing this single term to non-Euclidean topologies is identified as the core contribution.
sections.heading: BACKGROUND: EUCLIDEAN KD-TREE
sections.headline: A Euclidean KD-tree prunes with a per-dimension squared gap to the split value, and generalizing that term is the core contribution.

sections.body: The user declares the space as a product of base manifolds, and the metric is a weighted squared sum over blocks. Each scalar coordinate gets a topology tag: Linear, Circular or Quaternion. The per-coordinate lower bound `g_i` is the squared point-to-interval distance for linear coordinates, the wrapped endpoint distance for circular coordinates, and the smaller of two linear bounds against v and -v for quaternion blocks. Lemma 1 states that the summed bound never exceeds the minimum squared distance to data in the region, so pruning is exact. For quaternion blocks, a tighter block bound is reconstructed from the stored split intervals at the prune gate, with no per-node storage. The section also notes that the circle's plus-or-minus pi seam requires carrying the region down the recursion rather than using a single cut value.
sections.heading: EXACT NN ON PRODUCT MANIFOLDS
sections.headline: A coordinate-wise admissible bound, wrap-aware for circles and double-cover-aware for quaternions, makes pruning exact on product manifolds.

sections.body: This section describes an incremental index for changing point sets, such as sliding-window LiDAR maps. It keeps one self-balancing tree with one point per node, plus subtree size, tombstone count and a subtree bounding box. Deletes are lazy tombstones. Weight-balanced partial rebuilds reclaim tombstoned nodes through a pooled free-list. An optional background thread rebuilds large near-root subtrees, while the foreground replays an operation log onto the new tree before swapping it in. The index applies the same manifold bound to its subtree boxes, so it stays exact on product manifolds under churn. The section states that the asynchronous mode roughly doubles memory.
sections.heading: INCREMENTAL SELF-BALANCING INDEX
sections.headline: An incremental single tree with lazy deletes and pooled memory supports changing point sets, with an optional asynchronous rebuild mode.

sections.body: The section reports several experiments. On KITTI Velodyne scans, the library answers exact 1-NN queries in 1.17 µs at N=2×10^6, against 1.08 µs for `pico_tree`. On SO(2), S^2, SO(3), SE(3) and a two-rotation product at N=10^6, the proposed tree matches the exhaustive ground truth with recall 1.0. Its speedups over brute force are 1399 on SO(2), 27.6 on SO(3), 54.7 on SE(3) and 8.7 on the two-rotation product. On SO(3), all of MPNN, nigh and the proposed tree return recall 1.0. A sliding-window test on a 4.8 M-point map reports a synchronous median update of 93 ms.
sections.heading: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.headline: Exact search returns recall 1.0 against brute force, while a Euclidean tree on raw coordinates drops to 0.26 with two quaternion blocks.

sections.body: The conclusions summarize the library as an exact product-manifold KD-tree with no per-node storage, plus an incremental index. The authors state that exactness holds with respect to the product metric, whose rotational factor is chordal. For a single rotation or sphere factor, they note, the ordering is geodesic. They report speedups over brute force on spaces relevant to robotics, and state that the common workarounds lose loop closures on real trajectories. The incremental index is reported to beat the ikd-Tree on update latency, at single-tree query speed and with bounded memory.
sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.headline: The library gives exact product-manifold search with no per-node storage, and its incremental index beats ikd-Tree on update latency.
